newsitem.title: ITALY: San Paolo offer kicks off, shares dip.
newsitem.headline: San Paolo offer kicks off, shares dip.

text.p: San Paolo di Torino kicked off a week-long stock offering on Monday which will transfer majority control of Italy's biggest bank from a foundation to the public market through the sale of a total 26.96 percent stake .

This is the second tranche sold by the controlling foundation, Turin-based Compagnia di San Paolo. It first sold 35 percent in 1992. This week's offer may be aided by a downward drift in the bank's share price, tempting private and institutional investors.
The sale runs until Friday May 23, and is expected to raise 2.4 trillion lire ($1.4 billion) though the final price will only be set at the end of the week.

San Paolo shares closed down 4.53 percent at 10,610 lire in an easier Milan stock market, as the stock went ex-dividend. This compared to some 11,800 lire a month ago, and a 12,200 lire price of San Paolo's initial offering at the bank's first offering in 1992.

Banking analysts believe the share price may have to dip lower throughout the week to make the offer more attractive to investors, while the foundation is keen to sell above 10,000 lire per share -- the value of the stake in its books.

They are balancing the positive impact of San Paolo's moves over the last 18 months to modernise its operations against the poor record of Italian banking and San Paolo's exposure to the property sector -- both its own investments and loans granted.

The bank announced late last week a maximum price for the new issue at 10,850 lire per share, while the final price will be fixed at the end of this week based either on Friday's closing price minus a 2.5 percent price discount or the maximum price, whichever is lower.

Analysts said the offer could be attractive to investors who are focusing on possible improvements in the pipeline due changes at the Turin-based bank, but pricing will be critical after the first offer in 1992 was seen to be priced too high.

"There is huge potential for improvement in the Italian banking sector and so there are good grounds for participation in this offer," said banking industry analyst Derek Chambers at brokers HSBC James Capel in London.

However, many analysts say the offer needs to be priced below 10,500 lire to attract large investor interest, while some more critical analysts say the price needs to be nearer 10,000 lire before they would advise investors to buy.

But they pointed out that core shareholders such as Spain's Banco Santander and Italian investment bank IMI exercised options to increase their holdings at 10,300 lire, and would not be happy at being undercut by buyers in this public offering.

The bank has already conducted a private placement of 20 percent of San Paolo to such groups bringing the foundation's stake to 45.6 percent, and after the public issue the stake will fall below 20 percent.

A Milan-based banking analyst pointed out that he would not advise buying much above 10,000 lire, since San Paolo has not seen the radical structural changes such as Credito Italiano and still has property problem investments and loans.

He pointed out that the bank's management has not changed substantial since the first "over-priced" offering in 1992, and the main attraction of the offer was the one free share for public investors for each ten new shares they hold for one year.
The full public offer is for 220 million shares, while there will be a "green shoe" extra allocation of 33 million shares for institutions if the issue is oversubscribed.
In addition, the Italian Treasury, the Italy state railway and another related bank will sell most of their combined 7.4 percent stake adding to the public offer. ($1=1,673 lire)
